nodes.name: Lemma 5.2
nodes.statement: Suppose that $Q$ admits a Lebesgue density $f$, where $f$ is globally Lipschitz and has a compact support $\overline{\{f>0\}}$. If $(\Theta,(H_n)_{n\in\NN})$ satisfies the assumptions of Theorem \ref{th2a}, then there exist $n_0=n_0(f,\Theta)\in\NN$ and $C=C(f,\Theta)\in(0,\infty)$ such that \begin{equation} \bigl\|\LLL_\theta (Y_{1,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} )-\LLL_\theta (Y_{2,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} ) \bigr\| \le \frac {C^k}n \end{equation} for all $\theta\in\Theta$, $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$ and $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$.
nodes.statement_short: For Lipschitz compactly supported densities, the conditional laws of the two GARCH families differ by at most $C^k/n$ in total variation.
assumptions: Suppose that $Q$ admits a Lebesgue density $f$, where $f$ is globally Lipschitz and has a compact support $\overline{\{f>0\}}$
If $(\Theta,(H_n)_{n\in\NN})$ satisfies the assumptions of Theorem \ref{th2a}
conclusions: \bigl\|\LLL_\theta (Y_{1,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} )-\LLL_\theta (Y_{2,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} ) \bigr\| \le \frac {C^k}n

nodes.name: Invoke Lemma 5.1 on the compact support of $f$
nodes.statement: By assumption, we have $f(x)=0$ for all $|x|\ge S$ and some $S>0$. Hence, there are $n_0=n_0(f,\theta)\in\NN$ and $C_1=C_1(f,\theta)\in(1,\infty)$ such that for $C$ replaced by $C_1$, the assertion of Lemma \ref{Lemexpectbound} holds.
nodes.statement_short: Compact support gives an $S$ with $Q([-S,S])=1$, so Lemma 5.1 applies with a constant $C_1$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.2
nodes.statement:
By assumption, we have $f(x)=0$ for all $|x|\ge S$ and some $S>0$. Hence, there are $n_0=n_0(f,	heta)\in\NN$ and $C_1=C_1(f,	heta)\in(1,\infty)$ such that for $C$ replaced by $C_1$, the assertion of Lemma ef{Lemexpectbound} holds. Let $n\ge n_0$, $i=1,2$, $	heta\in\Theta$, $1 \le k \le n$ and $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$. Recall \eqref{defhatg}. In view of \eqref{awayfromzero}, $\Psi_{i,n,	heta}\dvtx\RR^k	o\RR^k$ is a\vadjust{\goodbreak} well defined $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism, where $\Psi_{i,n,\sigma,	heta}=(\psi_{i,n,l,\sigma,	heta})_{1\le l\le k}\dvtx reak\RR^k	o\RR^k$ is defined by  egin{eqnarray} \psi_{i,n,l,\sigma,	heta}(y)= rac{y_l}{\hat g^{1/2}_{i,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y)} \end{eqnarray} for $y=(y_1,\dots,y_k)\in\RR^k$ and $1\le l\le k$. For all $n\ge n_0$, $	heta\in\Theta$, $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$ and $\sigma \in M_{n,k}$, we define \[ 	ilde f_{i,n,k,\sigma,	heta}(y) = \prod_{l=1}^k  rac{f(\psi_{i,n,l,\sigma,	heta}(y))}{\hat g^{1/2}_{i,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y)},\qquad y\in\RR^k , i=1,2 . \] It follows from \eqref{defhatg}, \eqref{Yip} and \eqref{Phiip} that $	ilde f_{i,n,k,\sigma,	heta}$ is a density of the probability measure $\LLL_	heta (Y_{i,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} )$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure $\ell^{\otimes k}$ on $\BBB(\RR^k)$. In particular, we must have  egin{equation}  igl\|\LLL_	heta (Y_{1,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} ) -\LLL_	heta (Y_{2,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} )  igr\| =  rac 12\int_{\RR^k}|	ilde f_{1,n,k,\sigma,	heta}(y)-	ilde f_{2,n,k,\sigma,	heta}(y)|\,\mathrm{d}y \end{equation} for all $	heta\in\Theta$, $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$ and $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$. Suppose that $C_f\in(0,\infty)$ is a global Lipschitz constant of $f$. By means of simple substitutions, for all $\epsilon>0$ and $w, v\ge\epsilon$, we can observe that \[  rac 12 \int  iggl| rac{f(x/v)}{v}- rac{f(x/w)}{w}  iggr|\,\mathrm{d}x \le  rac1 \epsilon (S^2 C_f+1) |v-w| . \] Consequently, for all $\epsilon>0$, we find a $\kappa_1=\kappa_1(f,\epsilon)\in(1,\infty)$ such that \[  rac12 \int  iggl| rac{f(x/v)}{v}- rac{f(x/w)}{w}  iggr|\,\mathrm{d}x \le \kappa_1(\epsilon)|v-w|,\qquad v,w\ge\epsilon . \] In view of \eqref{awayfromzero}, there thus exists some $\kappa_2=\kappa_2(f,\Theta)\in(1,\infty)$ such that  egin{eqnarray} && rac12 \int  iggl| rac{f(y_l/\hat g^{1/2}_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y))}{\hat g_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}^{1/2}(y)}-  rac{f(y_l/\hat g^{1/2}_{2,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y))}{\hat g^{1/2}_{2,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y)}  iggr|\,\mathrm{d}y_l
onumber\ [-8pt]\ [-8pt] &&\quad\le\kappa_2|\hat g_{1,n,{l - 1},\sigma,	heta}(y)-\hat g_{2,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y)|
onumber \end{eqnarray} for all $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$, $1 \le l\le k$, $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$, $y\in\RR^{k}$ and $	heta\in\Theta$. By integrating over $y_k$, we get from \eqref{cinproof} that  egin{eqnarray} && rac12\int_{\RR^k}|	ilde f_{1,n,k,\sigma,	heta}(y)-	ilde f_{2,n,k,\sigma,	heta}(y)|\,\mathrm{d}y
onumber\ &&\quad\le \kappa_2\int_{\RR^{k - 1}}\prod_{l=1}^{k-1}  rac{f(\psi_{1,n,l,\sigma,	heta}(y))}{\hat g^{1/2}_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y)} |\hat g_{1,n,k - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y)- \hat g_{2,n,k - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y) |\,\mathrm{d}y\ &&\qquad{} + rac12\int_{\RR^{k - 1}} \Biggl|\prod_{l=1}^{k-1}  rac{f(\psi_{1,n,l,\sigma,	heta}(y))}{\hat g^{1/2}_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y)}- \prod_{l=1}^{k-1}  rac{f(\psi_{2,n,l,\sigma,	heta}(y))}{\hat g^{1/2}_{2,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y)} \Biggr|\,\mathrm{d}y
onumber \end{eqnarray} for all $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$, $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$ and $	heta\in\Theta$. It follows from \eqref{hatcondEgdiff} that  egin{eqnarray} && \int_{\RR^{k - 1}}\prod_{l=1}^{k-1}  rac{f(\psi_{1,n,l,\sigma,	heta}(y))}{g^{1/2}_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma ,	heta}(y)} |\hat g_{1,n,k - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y)- \hat g_{2,n,k - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y) |\,\mathrm{d}y
onumber\ [-8pt]\ [-8pt] &&\quad=E_	heta [ |\hat g_{1,n,k - 1,	heta}(Y_{1,n})- \hat g_{2,n,k - 1,	heta}(Y_{1,n}) | |A_{n,k,\sigma}]\le  rac{C_1^k}n
onumber \end{eqnarray} for all $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$, $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$ and $	heta\in\Theta$. Let $C=\mathrm{e} \kappa_2 C_1$. By induction, we thus get from \eqref{hatg0diff} and \eqref{cinproof2}--\eqref{cinproof3} that \[  igl \|\LLL_	heta (Y_{1,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} )-\LLL _	heta (Y_{2,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} )  igr\| \le rac{C^k}{n} , \] uniformly for all $n\,{\ge}\,n_0, 1\,{\le}\,k\,{\le}\,n, \sigma\,{\in}\,M_{n,k}$ and $	heta\,{\in}\,\Theta$. This completes the proof of the~lemma.\vspace*{-3pt}
nodes.statement_short: Write the conditional laws as explicit product densities via a diffeomorphism, then bound their $L^1$ distance by Lipschitz continuity and induction.

nodes.name: The normalizing map $\Psi_{i,n,\sigma,\theta}$ is a diffeomorphism
nodes.statement: Let $n\ge n_0$, $i=1,2$, $\theta\in\Theta$, $1 \le k \le n$ and $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$. Recall \eqref{defhatg}. In view of \eqref{awayfromzero}, $\Psi_{i,n,\theta}\dvtx\RR^k\to\RR^k$ is a\vadjust{\goodbreak} well defined $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism, where $\Psi_{i,n,\sigma,\theta}=(\psi_{i,n,l,\sigma,\theta})_{1\le l\le k}\dvtx\break\RR^k\to\RR^k$ is defined by \begin{eqnarray} \psi_{i,n,l,\sigma,\theta}(y)=\frac{y_l}{\hat g^{1/2}_{i,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y)} \end{eqnarray} for $y=(y_1,\dots,y_k)\in\RR^k$ and $1\le l\le k$.
nodes.statement_short: Dividing each coordinate by $\hat g^{1/2}$ is smooth and invertible because $\hat g$ is bounded away from zero.

nodes.name: Explicit product densities of the conditional laws
nodes.statement: For all $n\ge n_0$, $\theta\in\Theta$, $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$ and $\sigma \in M_{n,k}$, we define \[ \tilde f_{i,n,k,\sigma,\theta}(y) = \prod_{l=1}^k \frac{f(\psi_{i,n,l,\sigma,\theta}(y))}{\hat g^{1/2}_{i,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y)},\qquad y\in\RR^k , i=1,2 . \] It follows from \eqref{defhatg}, \eqref{Yip} and \eqref{Phiip} that $\tilde f_{i,n,k,\sigma,\theta}$ is a density of the probability measure $\LLL_\theta (Y_{i,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} )$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure $\ell^{\otimes k}$ on $\BBB(\RR^k)$. In particular, we must have \begin{equation} \bigl\|\LLL_\theta (Y_{1,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} ) -\LLL_\theta (Y_{2,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} ) \bigr\| = \frac 12\int_{\RR^k}|\tilde f_{1,n,k,\sigma,\theta}(y)-\tilde f_{2,n,k,\sigma,\theta}(y)|\,\mathrm{d}y \end{equation} for all $\theta\in\Theta$, $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$ and $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$.
nodes.statement_short: The conditional law of $Y_{i,n}$ has density $\prod_l f(\psi_{i,n,l})/\hat g^{1/2}_{i,n,l-1}$, so the distance is an $L^1$ integral.

nodes.name: Lipschitz bound for scale perturbations of $f$
nodes.statement: Suppose that $C_f\in(0,\infty)$ is a global Lipschitz constant of $f$. By means of simple substitutions, for all $\epsilon>0$ and $w, v\ge\epsilon$, we can observe that \[ \frac 12 \int \biggl|\frac{f(x/v)}{v}-\frac{f(x/w)}{w} \biggr|\,\mathrm{d}x \le \frac1 \epsilon (S^2 C_f+1) |v-w| . \] Consequently, for all $\epsilon>0$, we find a $\kappa_1=\kappa_1(f,\epsilon)\in(1,\infty)$ such that \[ \frac12 \int \biggl|\frac{f(x/v)}{v}-\frac{f(x/w)}{w} \biggr|\,\mathrm{d}x \le \kappa_1(\epsilon)|v-w|,\qquad v,w\ge\epsilon . \]
nodes.statement_short: For scales bounded below, $\frac12\int|f(x/v)/v-f(x/w)/w|\,\mathrm{d}x\le\kappa_1|v-w|$.

nodes.name: Apply the scale bound coordinatewise
nodes.statement: In view of \eqref{awayfromzero}, there thus exists some $\kappa_2=\kappa_2(f,\Theta)\in(1,\infty)$ such that \begin{eqnarray} &&\frac12 \int \biggl|\frac{f(y_l/\hat g^{1/2}_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y))}{\hat g_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}^{1/2}(y)}- \frac{f(y_l/\hat g^{1/2}_{2,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y))}{\hat g^{1/2}_{2,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y)} \biggr|\,\mathrm{d}y_l\nonumber\\ [-8pt]\\ [-8pt] &&\quad\le\kappa_2|\hat g_{1,n,{l - 1},\sigma,\theta}(y)-\hat g_{2,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y)|\nonumber \end{eqnarray} for all $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$, $1 \le l\le k$, $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$, $y\in\RR^{k}$ and $\theta\in\Theta$.
nodes.statement_short: Each coordinate contributes at most $\kappa_2|\hat g_{1}-\hat g_{2}|$.

nodes.name: Peel off the last coordinate
nodes.statement: By integrating over $y_k$, we get from \eqref{cinproof} that \begin{eqnarray} &&\frac12\int_{\RR^k}|\tilde f_{1,n,k,\sigma,\theta}(y)-\tilde f_{2,n,k,\sigma,\theta}(y)|\,\mathrm{d}y\nonumber\\ &&\quad\le \kappa_2\int_{\RR^{k - 1}}\prod_{l=1}^{k-1} \frac{f(\psi_{1,n,l,\sigma,\theta}(y))}{\hat g^{1/2}_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y)} |\hat g_{1,n,k - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y)- \hat g_{2,n,k - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y) |\,\mathrm{d}y\\ &&\qquad{} +\frac12\int_{\RR^{k - 1}} \Biggl|\prod_{l=1}^{k-1} \frac{f(\psi_{1,n,l,\sigma,\theta}(y))}{\hat g^{1/2}_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y)}- \prod_{l=1}^{k-1} \frac{f(\psi_{2,n,l,\sigma,\theta}(y))}{\hat g^{1/2}_{2,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y)} \Biggr|\,\mathrm{d}y\nonumber \end{eqnarray} for all $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$, $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$ and $\theta\in\Theta$.
nodes.statement_short: Integrating in $y_k$ splits the $L^1$ distance into a $\hat g$-gap term and a $(k-1)$-dimensional remainder.

nodes.name: Identify the gap term as a conditional expectation
nodes.statement: It follows from \eqref{hatcondEgdiff} that \begin{eqnarray} && \int_{\RR^{k - 1}}\prod_{l=1}^{k-1} \frac{f(\psi_{1,n,l,\sigma,\theta}(y))}{g^{1/2}_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma ,\theta}(y)} |\hat g_{1,n,k - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y)- \hat g_{2,n,k - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y) |\,\mathrm{d}y\nonumber\\ [-8pt]\\ [-8pt] &&\quad=E_\theta [ |\hat g_{1,n,k - 1,\theta}(Y_{1,n})- \hat g_{2,n,k - 1,\theta}(Y_{1,n}) | |A_{n,k,\sigma}]\le \frac{C_1^k}n\nonumber \end{eqnarray} for all $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$, $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$ and $\theta\in\Theta$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.1(iii) bounds it by $C_1^k/n$.

nodes.name: Induction on the dimension $k$
nodes.statement: Let $C=\mathrm{e} \kappa_2 C_1$. By induction, we thus get from \eqref{hatg0diff} and \eqref{cinproof2}--\eqref{cinproof3} that \[ \bigl \|\LLL_\theta (Y_{1,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} )-\LLL _\theta (Y_{2,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} ) \bigr\| \le\frac{C^k}{n} , \] uniformly for all $n\,{\ge}\,n_0, 1\,{\le}\,k\,{\le}\,n, \sigma\,{\in}\,M_{n,k}$ and $\theta\,{\in}\,\Theta$. This completes the proof of the~lemma.\vspace*{-3pt}
nodes.statement_short: Iterating the peeling bound gives the claimed $C^k/n$ estimate uniformly.

nodes.name: Approximate $f$ by Lipschitz compactly supported densities $h_m$
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a Lebesgue density of $Q$ and $\Theta$ be as in Theorem \ref{th2a}. We denote the positive part of a function $g\dvtx\RR\to\RR$ by $g^+$. Let $C^\infty_C$ be the space of infinitely often continuously differentiable functions $g\dvtx\RR\to\RR$ with compact support $\overline{\{g>0\}}$. As $C^\infty_C$ is dense in $L^1$, we find a sequence of $g_m\in C_C^\infty$, $m\in\NN$, such that $\int|g_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell\to0$ as $m\to\infty$. It is immediate that both $\int|g_m^+-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell\to0$ and $\int g_m^+\,\mathrm{d}\ell\to1$ as $m\to \infty$. Without loss of generality, we may thus assume that $\int g_m^+\,\mathrm{d}\ell>0$ for all $m\in\NN$. Then, $h_m:=g^+_m/\int g_m^+\,\mathrm{d}\ell$ defines a sequence of globally Lipschitz continuous probability densities with a compact support $\overline{\{h_m>0\}}$ such that $\int|h_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell\to0$.
nodes.statement_short: Density of $C_C^\infty$ in $L^1$ gives probability densities $h_m\to f$ in $L^1$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.2 (part II)
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a Lebesgue density of $Q$ and $\Theta$ be as in Theorem \ref{th2a}. We denote the positive part of a function $g\dvtx\RR\to\RR$ by $g^+$. Let $C^\infty_C$ be the space of infinitely often continuously differentiable functions $g\dvtx\RR\to\RR$ with compact support $\overline{\{g>0\}}$. As $C^\infty_C$ is dense in $L^1$, we find a sequence of $g_m\in C_C^\infty$, $m\in\NN$, such that $\int|g_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell\to0$ as $m\to\infty$. It is immediate that both $\int|g_m^+-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell\to0$ and $\int g_m^+\,\mathrm{d}\ell\to1$ as $m\to \infty$. Without loss of generality, we may thus assume that $\int g_m^+\,\mathrm{d}\ell>0$ for all $m\in\NN$. Then, $h_m:=g^+_m/\int g_m^+\,\mathrm{d}\ell$ defines a sequence of globally Lipschitz continuous probability densities with a compact support $\overline{\{h_m>0\}}$ such that $\int|h_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell\to0$. For $m\in\NN$, let $Z^{(m)}_n=(Z^{(m)}_{n,k})_{1\le k\le n}$ be a random vector with distribution \[ \LLL\bigl(Z^{(m)}_n\bigr)(B) = \biggl((1 - p_n)\varepsilon_0(B)+p_n \int _Bh_m\,\mathrm{d}\ell \biggr)^{\otimes n} , \] with $B\in\BBB(\RR^n)$, $m,n\in\NN$, $1\le k\le n$. If we replace $Z_{n,k}$ by $Z^{(m)}_{n,k}$ in \eqref{Xip}, then we get yet another family of GARCH models, $X^{(m)}_{i,n}=(X^{(m)}_{i,n}(k))_{1\le k\le n}$, say, indexed by $\theta\in\Theta$, $i=1,2$ and $m$, $n\in\NN$. It follows from the monotonicity theorem for Markov kernels and a well-known upper bound for product measures (see \cite{Re93}, Lemma 1.4.2(i) and page 23) that for all \mbox{$i=1,2$}, \begin{eqnarray} \hspace*{-15pt}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\bigl\|\LLL_\theta(X_{i,n})-\LLL _\theta\bigl(X^{(m)}_{i,n}\bigr)\bigr\| &\le& \bigl\|\LLL(Z_{n})-\LLL\bigl(Z^{(m)}_n\bigr)\bigr\|\nonumber\\ [-8pt]\\ [-8pt] \hspace*{-15pt}&\le& n\bigl\|\LLL(Z_{n,1})-\LLL\bigl(Z^{(m)}_{n,1}\bigr)\bigr\|= \frac{n p_n}2 \int|h_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell .\nonumber \end{eqnarray}\looseness=0 As $h_m$ is globally Lipschitz with a compact support $\overline{\{h_m>0\}}$ for all $m\in\NN_0$, the assumptions of Lemma \ref{condTVlem} hold. For all $m\in\NN$, there thus exist $n_m\in\NN$ and $C_m=C(h_m,\Theta)\in(0,\infty)$ such that for all $n\ge n_m$, we get, by conditioning and the monotonicity theorem for Markov kernels, that \begin{equation} \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\bigl\|\LLL_\theta \bigl(X^{(m)}_{1,n}\bigr)-\LLL_\theta\bigl(X^{(m)}_{2,n}\bigr)\bigr\| \le \frac 1n E \bigl[C_m^{\|N_n\|} \bigr] \end{equation} for $N_n$ as defined in \eqref{defNn}. Recall \eqref{Xip}. By combining \eqref{truncatednoise} and \eqref{condTV1}, we get, from the triangle inequality, that \[ \sup_{\theta\in\Theta} \bigl\|\LLL_\theta(G_n)-\LLL_\theta \bigl(G_n^{(0)}\bigr) \bigr\| \le n p_n \int|h_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell+\frac1n E \bigl[C_m^{\|N_n\|} \bigr] \] for all $m\in\NN$ and $n\ge n_m$. As \eqref{lre} holds, we have $\lim_{n\to\infty}EC_m^{\|N_n\|}= e^{\lambda(C_m-1)}$ and thus \[ \limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta} \bigl\|\LLL_\theta (G_n)-\LLL_\theta\bigl(G_n^{(0)}\bigr) \bigr\| \le\lambda \limsup_{m\to\infty}\int|h_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell=0 , \] giving \eqref{th2astronger}. This completes the proof of Theorem \ref{th2a} in the case where $Q_n=Q$ for all $n\in\NN$ (see \eqref{QnequalsQ}). Now, assume that $Q_n\to Q$ in total variation norm as $n\to\infty$. For $m\in\NN$, let $\widehat Z_n=(\widehat Z_{n,k})_{1\le k\le n}$ be a random vector with distribution \[ \LLL(\widehat Z_n) = \bigl((1 - p_n)\varepsilon_0+p_n Q_n \bigr)^{\otimes n},\qquad n\in\NN . \] If we replace $Z_{n,k}$ by $\widehat Z_{n,k}$ in \eqref{Xip}, then we get the GARCH models in the assertion of the theorem. We denote them by $\widehat X_{i,n}$, $n\in\NN$, $i=1,2$. By the same argument as in~\eqref{truncatednoise}, we must have, for all $i=1,2$ and $n\in\NN$ , \[ \sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\|\LLL_\theta(\widehat {X}_{i,n})-\LLL_\theta(X_{i,n})\| \le np_n\|Q_n-Q\| . \] As the right-hand side tends to zero, this completes the proof of the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $f$ in $L^1$ by Lipschitz compactly supported densities, apply Lemma 5.2 to the truncated models, then pass to the limit.

nodes.name: Define the truncated innovation vectors and GARCH families
nodes.statement: For $m\in\NN$, let $Z^{(m)}_n=(Z^{(m)}_{n,k})_{1\le k\le n}$ be a random vector with distribution \[ \LLL\bigl(Z^{(m)}_n\bigr)(B) = \biggl((1 - p_n)\varepsilon_0(B)+p_n \int _Bh_m\,\mathrm{d}\ell \biggr)^{\otimes n} , \] with $B\in\BBB(\RR^n)$, $m,n\in\NN$, $1\le k\le n$. If we replace $Z_{n,k}$ by $Z^{(m)}_{n,k}$ in \eqref{Xip}, then we get yet another family of GARCH models, $X^{(m)}_{i,n}=(X^{(m)}_{i,n}(k))_{1\le k\le n}$, say, indexed by $\theta\in\Theta$, $i=1,2$ and $m$, $n\in\NN$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace $Q$ by $h_m\,\mathrm{d}\ell$ in the thinning mixture, giving models $X^{(m)}_{i,n}$.

nodes.name: Bound the truncation error uniformly in $\theta$
nodes.statement: It follows from the monotonicity theorem for Markov kernels and a well-known upper bound for product measures (see \cite{Re93}, Lemma 1.4.2(i) and page 23) that for all \mbox{$i=1,2$}, \begin{eqnarray} \hspace*{-15pt}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\bigl\|\LLL_\theta(X_{i,n})-\LLL _\theta\bigl(X^{(m)}_{i,n}\bigr)\bigr\| &\le& \bigl\|\LLL(Z_{n})-\LLL\bigl(Z^{(m)}_n\bigr)\bigr\|\nonumber\\ [-8pt]\\ [-8pt] \hspace*{-15pt}&\le& n\bigl\|\LLL(Z_{n,1})-\LLL\bigl(Z^{(m)}_{n,1}\bigr)\bigr\|= \frac{n p_n}2 \int|h_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell .\nonumber \end{eqnarray}\looseness=0
nodes.statement_short: Product-measure bounds give an error $\frac{np_n}{2}\int|h_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell$.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 5.2 to the truncated models
nodes.statement: As $h_m$ is globally Lipschitz with a compact support $\overline{\{h_m>0\}}$ for all $m\in\NN_0$, the assumptions of Lemma \ref{condTVlem} hold. For all $m\in\NN$, there thus exist $n_m\in\NN$ and $C_m=C(h_m,\Theta)\in(0,\infty)$ such that for all $n\ge n_m$, we get, by conditioning and the monotonicity theorem for Markov kernels, that \begin{equation} \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\bigl\|\LLL_\theta \bigl(X^{(m)}_{1,n}\bigr)-\LLL_\theta\bigl(X^{(m)}_{2,n}\bigr)\bigr\| \le \frac 1n E \bigl[C_m^{\|N_n\|} \bigr] \end{equation} for $N_n$ as defined in \eqref{defNn}.
nodes.statement_short: Conditioning on the jump pattern gives $\sup_\theta\|\LLL(X^{(m)}_{1,n})-\LLL(X^{(m)}_{2,n})\|\le E[C_m^{\|N_n\|}]/n$.

nodes.name: Combine by the triangle inequality and let $n,m\to\infty$
nodes.statement: Recall \eqref{Xip}. By combining \eqref{truncatednoise} and \eqref{condTV1}, we get, from the triangle inequality, that \[ \sup_{\theta\in\Theta} \bigl\|\LLL_\theta(G_n)-\LLL_\theta \bigl(G_n^{(0)}\bigr) \bigr\| \le n p_n \int|h_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell+\frac1n E \bigl[C_m^{\|N_n\|} \bigr] \] for all $m\in\NN$ and $n\ge n_m$. As \eqref{lre} holds, we have $\lim_{n\to\infty}EC_m^{\|N_n\|}= e^{\lambda(C_m-1)}$ and thus \[ \limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta} \bigl\|\LLL_\theta (G_n)-\LLL_\theta\bigl(G_n^{(0)}\bigr) \bigr\| \le\lambda \limsup_{m\to\infty}\int|h_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell=0 , \] giving \eqref{th2astronger}. This completes the proof of Theorem \ref{th2a} in the case where $Q_n=Q$ for all $n\in\NN$ (see \eqref{QnequalsQ}).
nodes.statement_short: The Poisson limit of $E[C_m^{\|N_n\|}]$ is finite, so the $1/n$ term vanishes and the uniform total-variation limit follows.

nodes.name: Relax $Q_n=Q$ to $\|Q_n-Q\|\to0$
nodes.statement: Now, assume that $Q_n\to Q$ in total variation norm as $n\to\infty$. For $m\in\NN$, let $\widehat Z_n=(\widehat Z_{n,k})_{1\le k\le n}$ be a random vector with distribution \[ \LLL(\widehat Z_n) = \bigl((1 - p_n)\varepsilon_0+p_n Q_n \bigr)^{\otimes n},\qquad n\in\NN . \] If we replace $Z_{n,k}$ by $\widehat Z_{n,k}$ in \eqref{Xip}, then we get the GARCH models in the assertion of the theorem. We denote them by $\widehat X_{i,n}$, $n\in\NN$, $i=1,2$. By the same argument as in~\eqref{truncatednoise}, we must have, for all $i=1,2$ and $n\in\NN$ , \[ \sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\|\LLL_\theta(\widehat {X}_{i,n})-\LLL_\theta(X_{i,n})\| \le np_n\|Q_n-Q\| . \] As the right-hand side tends to zero, this completes the proof of the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: The same product bound costs only $np_n\|Q_n-Q\|\to0$.

nodes.name: Preparations: innovations, uniform order statistics and $\nu_n$
nodes.statement: We first need to make some preparations. Let $Z=(Z_n)_{n\in\NN}$ and $U=(U_n)_{n\in\NN}$ be independent sequences of i.i.d. random variables such that $\LLL(Z_1)=Q$ with Lebesgue density~$f$ and $U_1$ is uniformly distributed on $(0,1)$. For $d\in\NN$, we denote the order statistics of $0,U_1,\ldots,U_d$ by $0=:U_{d,0}<U_{d,1}\le\cdots\le U_{d,d}$. For each $n\in\NN$, let $\nu_n$ be a Poisson random variable with parameter $\gamma_n>0$, independent of $Z$ and $U$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix independent i.i.d. sequences $Z,U$ and a Poisson count $\nu_n$ with parameter $\gamma_n$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.3
nodes.statement_short: Reduce equivalence to equality of Hellinger transforms, extract the $d=1$ identity by analyticity in $\gamma_n$, then contradict it by strict monotonicity in each of the five cases.

nodes.name: Jump representation of $N$ and the mark space $\widetilde\RR$
nodes.statement_short: Represent $N$ by its atoms and record the spacings and jump sizes of $G$ and $\widehat G$.

nodes.name: Reduce to the jump experiments $\FFF_n$ and $\widehat\FFF_n$
nodes.statement_short: Since $h_0>0$ all arrival times are observed, so the path experiments are equivalent to the jump-data experiments.

nodes.name: Construct the diffeomorphism $\Psi_{d,w,\theta}$ and the volatility recursions
nodes.statement:
Let $\widehat w_0=0$ and for $d>0$, set $\widehat w_d=(1/d,\dots,1/d)\in\RR^d$. Recall that $\Theta\subseteq(0,\infty)	imes[0,\infty)^3$ and pick $d\in\NN_0$, $	heta=(h_0, eta,\alpha,\lambda)\in\Theta$, $w=(w_1,\dots ,w_d)\in S_d\cup\{\widehat w_d\}$. We define a diffeomorphism $\Psi_{d,w,	heta}\dvtx\RR^d	o\RR^d$ as follows: if $d=0$, then let $\Psi_{d,w,	heta}=0$; otherwise, if $d>0$,~let \[ \Psi_{d,w,	heta}(z)= (h_{d,w,	heta,k}^{1/2}(z) z_k )_{1\le k\le d},\qquad z=(z_1,\dots,z_d)\in\RR^d , \] where for $2\le k\le d$, we recursively define  egin{eqnarray} h_{d,w,	heta,k}(z)&=& rac{ eta}{\alpha}(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha w_k})+ \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha w_k}(1+\lambda z_{k-1}^2) h_{d,w,	heta,k-1}(z) ,
onumber\ [-9pt]\ [-9pt] h_{d,w,	heta,1}(z)&\equiv&h_{d,w,	heta,1}= rac{ eta}{\alpha }(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha w_1})+ \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha w_1}h_{0},
onumber \end{eqnarray} provided $\alpha>0$ and otherwise, if $\alpha=0$, we set  egin{eqnarray} h_{d,	heta,w,k}(z)&=& eta w_k+ h_{d,	heta,w,k-1}(z)(1+\lambda z_{k-1}^2) ,
onumber \ [-9pt]\ [-9pt] h_{d,	heta,w,1}(z)&\equiv&h_{d,w,	heta,1}= eta w_1+ h_{0} .
onumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Given spacings $w$, the jump sizes are a smooth invertible function of the innovations.

nodes.name: Define the Hellinger transform $\HHH_{d,\theta_1,\theta_2,w}$
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a strictly positive Lebesgue density of $Q$ and set \begin{eqnarray*} &&\HHH_{d,\theta_1,\theta_2,w}(\zeta) \\[-2pt] &&\quad= \int_{\RR^d} ( |J_{\Psi^{-1}_{d,w,\theta _1}}(x)| f^{\otimes d}(\Psi^{-1}_{d,w,\theta_1}(x)) )^{ \zeta} ( |J_{\Psi^{-1}_{d,w,\theta_2}}(x)| f^{\otimes d}(\Psi^{-1}_{d,w,\theta_2}(x)) )^{ 1-\zeta}\,\mathrm{d}x \end{eqnarray*} for all $\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta$, $0 < \zeta < 1$, $w\in S_d\cup\{\widehat{w}_d\}$.
nodes.statement_short: The $\zeta$-Hellinger integral of the two jump-size densities at fixed spacings.

nodes.name: Equivalence is equality of Hellinger transformations
nodes.statement: To summarize, we have thus far shown that for all $n\in\NN$, equivalence of $\EEE_{\gamma_n,Q}(\Theta)$ and $\widehat\EEE_{\gamma_n,Q}(\Theta)$ in deficiency\vadjust{\goodbreak} is equivalent to equivalence of $\FFF_{n}$ and $\widehat\FFF_{n}$ in deficiency. For the remaining part, recall that the two experiments are equivalent in deficiency if and only if their corresponding Hellinger transformations are equal (see \cite{St85}, Corollary 53.8). By solving the differential equations in \eqref{COG} and \eqref{hatEEE}, we thus arrive at the following identity:\looseness=-1\vspace*{-1pt} \[ \sum_{d=1}^\infty\frac{\gamma_n^d\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma_n}}{d!} \HHH_{d,\theta_1,\theta_2,\widehat w_d}(\zeta) = \sum _{d=1}^\infty \frac{\gamma_n^d\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma_n}}{d!} \int_{S_d} \HHH_{d,\theta_1,\theta_2,w}(\zeta) \frac{\mathrm{d}w}{\ell ^{\otimes d}(S_d)}\vspace*{-2pt} \]\looseness=0 for all $\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta$, $0 < \zeta < 1$, $n\in\NN$.
nodes.statement_short: Equivalence in deficiency holds iff the Poisson-mixed Hellinger transforms with equal and with random spacings agree.

nodes.name: Separate the terms by analyticity in $\gamma_n$
nodes.statement: In the last display, the functions are analytical in $\gamma_n$; consequently, for all $d\in\NN$, $\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta$, $0 < \zeta < 1$, we must have\vspace*{-1pt} \begin{equation} \HHH_{d,\theta_1,\theta_2,\widehat w_d}(\zeta) = \int_{S_d} \HHH_{d,\theta_1,\theta_2,w}(\zeta) \frac{\mathrm{d}w}{\ell ^{\otimes d}(S_d)}.\vspace*{-2pt} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Analyticity in $\gamma_n$ (with $\gamma_n\neq\gamma$) forces the identity for each $d$ separately.

nodes.name: Specialize to $d=1$ and $\zeta=\zeta_0$
nodes.statement: Next, we return to the proof of the theorem. By our assumption, there exists $\zeta_0\in(0,1)$ such that, with $g_{f,\zeta_0}\dvtx(0,\infty)\to[0,1]$ as in \eqref{defgQz}, $g_{f, \zeta_0}$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1]$. As a result, $h\mapsto g_{f, \zeta_0}(\sqrt{h})$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1]$. For all $\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta$, define $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}\dvtx(0,1]\to(0,\infty)$ by $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(w):=h_{1,w,\theta_2,1}(1)/h_{1,w,\theta_1,1}(1)$ for $0 < w \le 1$. In particular, taking $d=1$ and $\zeta=\zeta_0$ in \eqref{centralidentitynoneq}, we must have\vspace*{-1pt} \begin{equation} g_{f,\zeta_0} \bigl\{\sqrt{H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(1)} \bigr\} = \int_{(0,1)} g_{f,\zeta_0} \bigl\{\sqrt{H_{\theta_1,\theta _2}(w)} \bigr\}\,\mathrm{d}w\vspace*{-2pt} \end{equation} for all $\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta$.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity of $h\mapsto g_{f,\zeta_0}(\sqrt h)$ plus the ratio $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}$ gives the key mean-value identity.

nodes.name: Parts (i) and (ii): $h_0$ and $\beta$
nodes.statement: (i) and (ii) For $i=1,2,$ let $\theta_i=(h_{0,i},\beta_i,\alpha,\lambda)\in\Theta$. Then,\vspace*{-1pt} \[ h^2_{1,w,\theta_1,1}(1) \mathrm{e}^{\alpha w} \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}w}H_{\theta _1,\theta_2}(w) = \beta_2 h_{0,1}-\beta_1 h_{0,2},\qquad 0< w\le 1 .\vspace*{-2pt} \] (Note that this formula extends to $\alpha=0$.) If $\beta_1 = \beta_2 > 0$ and $h_{0,1} > h_{0,2}$, then $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}$ is strictly increasing with $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(1) \le1$, contradicting \eqref{centralidentitynoneq2} since $h\mapsto g_{f, \zeta_0}(\sqrt{h})$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1]$. If $h_{0,1} = h_{0,2}$ and $\beta_2 < \beta_1$, then $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}$ is strictly decreasing with $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(0+)=1$, contradicting \eqref{centralidentitynoneq2} since $h\mapsto g_{f, \zeta_0}(\sqrt{h})$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1]$. Reversing the roles of parameters by replacing $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}$ with $H_{\theta_2,\theta_1}$, the previous reasoning extends to the remaining cases where either $\beta_1 = \beta_2 > 0$ and $h_{0,1} < h_{0,2}$, or $h_{0,1} = h_{0,2}$ and $\beta_2 > \beta_1$. This completes the proof of (i) and (ii).
nodes.statement_short: Strict monotonicity of $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}$ contradicts the identity unless $h_0$ and $\beta$ coincide.

nodes.name: Part (iii): $\alpha$ when $\beta=0$
nodes.statement: (iii) If $(h_{0},\beta,\alpha_1,\lambda),(h_{0},\beta,\alpha_2,\lambda)\in \Theta$ and $\beta=0$, then we have $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(w)=\mathrm{e}^{(\alpha_1-\alpha_2)w}$ for all $w\in(0,1]$. (Note that this formula extends to $\alpha_1=0$ or $\alpha_2=0$.) By the same arguments as in parts (i) and (ii), we get from \eqref{centralidentitynoneq2} that $\alpha_1=\alpha_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Then $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(w)=\mathrm{e}^{(\alpha_1-\alpha_2)w}$, forcing $\alpha_1=\alpha_2$.

nodes.name: Part (iv): $\alpha_1=0$ forces $\alpha_2=0$
nodes.statement: (iv) In view of (iii), we may assume that $\beta>0$. Contradicting the hypothesis, we assume that $\alpha_2>0$. It follows from the strict inequality $\mathrm{e}^x-1>x$, $x>0$, that\vspace*{-1pt} \begin{eqnarray*} (h_0+\beta w)^2 \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}w}H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(w) &=&\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha_2w} \biggl\{w(\beta^2 - \alpha_2\beta h_0)-h_0^2\alpha_2 - \frac{\beta^2}{\alpha_2} (\mathrm{e}^{\alpha_2w} - 1) \biggr\}\\[-1pt] &<&-\alpha_2 h_0 \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha_2 w}(h_0+w\beta) < 0\vspace*{-2pt} \end{eqnarray*} for all $w\in(0,1]$. Thus, $w\mapsto H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(w)$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,1]$ with $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(0+)=1$, contradicting \eqref{centralidentitynoneq2}. Thus, we must have $\alpha_2=0$.\vadjust{\goodbreak}
nodes.statement_short: Assuming $\alpha_2>0$ makes $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}$ strictly decreasing with $H(0+)=1$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Part (v): ordering of $\alpha$ forces $h_0>\beta/\alpha_1$
nodes.statement: (v) Let $(h_{0},\beta,\alpha_1,\lambda),(h_{0},\beta,\alpha_2,\lambda)\in \Theta$ with $\alpha_{2}>\alpha_{1}$. Without loss of generality, we may assume that $\beta > 0$. First, assume that $\beta/\alpha_2\le h_0\le \beta/\alpha_1$. Then, $\beta-\alpha_1 h_0\ge0$ and $\beta-\alpha_2 h_0\le0$. Note that we cannot simultaneously have that $\beta - \alpha_1 h_0=\beta - \alpha_2 h_0= 0$ such that \[ h_{1,w,\theta_1,1}^2 \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}w}H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(w) = (\beta - \alpha_2h_0)\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha_2 w}h_{1,w,\theta_1,1} -(\beta - \alpha_1h_0)\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha_1 w}h_{1,w,\theta_2,1}<0 \] for all $0<w\le1$. Consequently, $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}$ is strictly decreasing with $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(0+)=1$, contradicting \eqref{centralidentitynoneq2}. Second, let $h_0<\beta/\alpha_2$ and set \[ \psi(w):= (\beta-\alpha_2h_0)h_{1,w,\theta_1,1} -(\beta-\alpha_1h_0)\mathrm{e}^{-(\alpha_1-\alpha_2) w}h_{1,w,\theta_2,1},\qquad 0<w\le1 . \] As we have $\alpha_2>\alpha_1$ and $h_0<\beta/\alpha_2$, we must have that $\beta - \alpha_1h_0>\beta - \alpha_2h_0>0$ such~that \[ \psi'(w)=(\alpha_1 - \alpha_2)(\beta - \alpha_1h_0)\mathrm{e}^{-(\alpha _1 - \alpha_2) w}h_{d,w,\theta_2,1}<0,\qquad 0<w\le1 . \] Note that $\psi(0+)=(\alpha_1 - \alpha_2) h_0^2<0$ and thus $\psi(w)<0$ for all $0<w\le1$. Since\break $\mathrm{e}^{\alpha_2w }h_{d,w,\theta_1,1}^2 \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}w}H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(w)=\psi(w)<0$ for all $0 < w \le 1$, $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}$ is strictly decreasing with $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(0+)=1$, contradicting \eqref{centralidentitynoneq2}. This completes the proof of (v).\
nodes.statement_short: In both remaining regimes the derivative of $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}$ is negative, contradicting the identity.

nodes.name: Path notation: first jump time and one-sided derivatives
nodes.statement: For $f\in D_d[0,1]$, we write $\Delta f=f(t)-f(t-)$, $0\le t\le1$, with the convention that $\Delta f(0)=0$. With the usual convention $\inf\varnothing=\infty$, we define $T(f)=\inf\{t\in[0,1]\dvtx\Delta f_1(t)\neq0\}\wedge1$ for all $f=(f_1,f_2)\in D_2$. Let $S$ be the set of all functions $f\in D_2$ with $T(f)\in(0,1)$. Let $D''_{0}\subseteq D_2[0,1]$ be the set of all functions $f=(f_1,f_2)$ such that the right-hand derivatives~$f'_1(0+)$ and $f''_2(0+)$ exist in $\RR$. Further, let $D''_{0,T}\subseteq S\cap D_0''$ be the set of all functions $f=(f_1,f_2)$ such that the right-hand derivatives $f'_2(T(f)+)$ and $f''_2(T(f)+)$ exist in $\RR$.

nodes.statement:
For $f\in D_d[0,1]$, we write $\Delta f=f(t)-f(t-)$, $0\le t\le1$, with the convention that $\Delta f(0)=0$. With the usual convention $\inf\varnothing=\infty$, we define $T(f)=\inf\{t\in[0,1]\dvtx\Delta f_1(t)
eq0\}\wedge1$ for all $f=(f_1,f_2)\in D_2$. Let $S$ be the set of all functions $f\in D_2$ with $T(f)\in(0,1)$. eq0$, then we define \[ X(f) =  iggl(|f_2(0)|,  iggl| rac{(f_2'(0+))^2 - f_2(0)f_2''(0+)}{f'_2(0+)}  iggr|,  iggl| rac{f_2''(0+)}{f'_2(0+)}  iggr|,\infty  iggr) . \] For the remaining cases, we set $X(f)= (|f_2(0)|,\infty,\infty,\infty )$. nodes.name: Define the parameter-reading statistic $X(f)$ by cases
nodes.statement:
Let $f\in D_2$ with $T=T(f)$. If $f\in D''_{0,T}$ and $f'_2(0+)
eq0$, then we set \[ X(f) =  iggl(|f_2(0)|,  iggl| rac{(f_2'(0+))^2 - f_2(0)f_2''(0+)}{f'_2(0+)}  iggr|,  iggl| rac{f_2''(0+)}{f'_2(0+)}  iggr|, rac{|\Delta f_2(T)|}{(\Delta f_1(T))^2}  iggr) . \] If $f\in D''_{0,T}$, $f'_2(0+)= 0$ and $f'_2(T+)
eq0$, then we set \[ X(f) =  iggl(|f_2(0)|,  iggl| rac{(f_2'(T+))^2 - f_2(T)f_2''(T+)}{f'_2(T+)}  iggr|,  iggl| rac{f_2''(T+)}{f'_2(T+)}  iggr|, rac{|\Delta f_2(T)|}{(\Delta f_1(T))^2}  iggr) . \] If $f\in D''_{0,T}$, $f'(0+)=f'_2(T+)=0$ and $\Delta f_2(T)
eq0$, then we set \[ X(f) =  iggl(|f_2(0)|,0,0 , rac{|\Delta f_2(T)|}{(\Delta f_1(T))^2}  iggr) .\vadjust{\goodbreak} \] If $f\in D''_{0,T}$, $f'(0+)=f'_2(T+)=0$ and $\Delta f_2(T)= 0$, then we set $X(f)=(|f_2(0)|,\infty,\infty,0)$. If $f\in D''_{0} ackslash S$ and $f'_2(0+)
eq0$, then we define \[ X(f) =  iggl(|f_2(0)|,  iggl| rac{(f_2'(0+))^2 - f_2(0)f_2''(0+)}{f'_2(0+)}  iggr|,  iggl| rac{f_2''(0+)}{f'_2(0+)}  iggr|,\infty  iggr) . \] For the remaining cases, we set $X(f)= (|f_2(0)|,\infty,\infty,\infty )$.
nodes.statement_short: Recover $(h_0,\beta,\alpha,\lambda)$ from $f_2(0)$, its right derivatives, and the first jump ratio, with $\infty$ where recovery fails.

nodes.name: $X$ is measurable and pushes $\LLL_\theta(G,h)$ to $Q_\theta$
nodes.statement: Then, $X\dvtx D_2\to[0,\infty]^4$ is a $\DDD_2$-$\BBB([0,\infty]^4)$-measurable mapping. Since $Q(\{0\})=0$, it follows from \eqref{COG} that $\LLL_\theta^X((G,h))=Q_{\theta}$ for all $\theta\in[0,\infty)^4$ and thus $\delta(\EEE_{h},\FFF)=0$ by \eqref{defMarkov}, where $\FFF$ is the experiment as defined in the assertion of the proposition.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $\delta(\EEE_h,\FFF)=0$.

nodes.name: Define the truncation map $\xi$ for the converse direction
nodes.statement: Next, we show that $\delta(\FFF,\EEE_h)=0$. To this end, we define $\xi=(\xi_1,\dots,\xi_3)\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\to[0,\infty)^3$ as follows. Let $\omega=(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_4)\in[0,\infty]^4$. If $(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_3)\in[0,\infty)^3$, then we set $\xi(\omega)=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3)$; if $\omega_1\in [0,\infty)$ and either $\omega_2=\infty$ or $\omega_3=\infty$, then we set $\xi(\omega)=(\omega_1,0,0)$; otherwise, we set $\xi(\omega)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Map the possibly infinite coordinates back into $[0,\infty)^3$.

nodes.name: Define the solution map $\Psi$ and the kernel $K_2$
nodes.statement: In the notation of the \hyperref[s1]{Introduction}, we define $\Psi: [0,\infty)^3\times\MM_2\to D_2$, where, for $0\le t\le1$, $\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3)\in[0,\infty)^3$ and $\sigma\in\MM_2$, $(f_1(t),f_2(t))=\Psi[\omega,\sigma](t)$ is defined to be the unique solution of the system of the following integral equations: \begin{eqnarray} \hspace*{-15pt}f_1(t) & = & \int_{[0,t]\times\RR^2} f_2^{1/2}(s-)z_1 \sigma(\mathrm{d}s,\mathrm{d}z_1,\mathrm{d}z_2) ,\nonumber \\ [-8pt]\\ [-8pt] \hspace*{-15pt}f_2(t) & = & \omega_1 + \int_{[0,t]}\bigl(\omega_2-\omega_3 f_2(s-)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}s + \int_{[0,t]\times\RR\times(0,\infty)} f_2(s-)z_2^2 \sigma(\mathrm{d}s,\mathrm{d}z_1,\mathrm{d}z_2) .\nonumber \end{eqnarray} Clearly, $\Psi$ is $(\BBB([0,\infty)^3)\otimes\MMM_2)/\DDD_2$-measurable and thus defines a deterministic Markov kernel $K_2\dvtx([0,\infty)^3\times\MM_2)\times\DDD_2\to[0,1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Solving the COGARCH system from $(\omega,\sigma)$ is measurable, hence a deterministic Markov kernel.

nodes.name: Define the randomization kernel $K_1$
nodes.statement_short: Regenerate the driving point measure with the recovered jump-scaling parameter, conditioned to be non-trivial.

nodes.name: $K_2K_1Q_\theta=\LLL_\theta(G,h)$ gives $\delta(\FFF,\EEE_h)=0$
nodes.statement: Observe that $K_2K_1Q_{\theta}=\LLL_{\theta}(G,h)$ for all $\theta\in[0,\infty)^4$, in view of \eqref{COG}. Hence, $\delta(\FFF,\EEE_h)=0$, by~\eqref{defMarkov}.
nodes.statement_short: The two kernels reconstruct the COGARCH law from the reference experiment.

nodes.name: Same argument for $\widehat\EEE_h$
nodes.statement: To summarize, we have shown that $\EEE_h$ is equivalent to $\FFF$ in deficiency. By means of similar arguments, we can show that $\Delta(\FFF,\widehat\EEE_h)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Symmetric reasoning gives $\Delta(\FFF,\widehat\EEE_h)=0$.

nodes.statement: For all $n\ge5$, we define a mapping $X_n\dvtx[\RR^{n + 1}]^2\to[0,\infty]^4$ as follows: fix $(x,y)\in[\RR^{n + 1}]^2$ and set $T=T_n(x,y)$. nodes.statement: (i) Define $X,X_n\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\to[0,\infty]^4$ as follows. If $\omega=(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_4)\in[0,\infty)^3\times\{\infty\} $ such that $\omega_1\omega_3=\omega_2$, then set $X(\omega)=(\omega_1,\infty,\infty,\infty)$; otherwise, set $X(\omega)=\omega$. If $\omega=(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_4)\in [0,\infty)^3\times\{\infty\}$ such that $\omega_1 n(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\omega_3/n})=\omega_2$, then set $X_n(\omega)=(\omega_1,\infty,\infty,\infty)$; otherwise, set $X_n(\omega)=\omega$, $n\in\NN$.
nodes.statement_short: Collapse the exceptional-point coordinates to $\infty$ according to $\Theta_e$ resp. $\Theta_{e,n}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.3
nodes.statement: (i) Define $X,X_n\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\to[0,\infty]^4$ as follows. If $\omega=(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_4)\in[0,\infty)^3\times\{\infty\} $ such that $\omega_1\omega_3=\omega_2$, then set $X(\omega)=(\omega_1,\infty,\infty,\infty)$; otherwise, set $X(\omega)=\omega$. If $\omega=(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_4)\in [0,\infty)^3\times\{\infty\}$ such that $\omega_1 n(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\omega_3/n})=\omega_2$, then set $X_n(\omega)=(\omega_1,\infty,\infty,\infty)$; otherwise, set $X_n(\omega)=\omega$, $n\in\NN$. By definition, the deficiency is non-decreasing in the parameter set with respect to set inclusions. Further, we have $\widehat Q^X_{\theta}=Q_{\theta}$ and $\widehat Q^{X_n}_{\theta}= Q_{\theta,n}$ for all $n\in\NN$ and thus, by~\eqref{defMarkov}, $\delta(\widehat\FFF(\Theta),\FFF(\Theta))\le \delta(\widehat\FFF,\FFF)=0$ and $\delta(\widehat\FFF(\Theta),\FFF_n(\Theta))\le \delta(\widehat\FFF,\FFF_n)=0$ for all $n\in\NN$, completing the proof of (i). (ii) First, assume that $\Theta$ satisfies \eqref{hsgleichbetaalphagleich} for all $x>0$. Without loss of generality, we may assume that $\Theta\subseteq[0,\infty)^4$ is a finite set (see \cite{St85}, Theorem 51.4). Define $\Omega_\Theta$ to be the set of all $\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\omega_4) \in(0,\infty)\times\{\infty\}^2\times\{0,\infty\}$ such that $( \omega_1,\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in(\Theta\cap\Theta_e)\backslash \widehat\Theta_e$ for some $(\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in[0,\infty)^3$. If $\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\omega_4)\in\Omega_\Theta$, then it follows from \eqref{hsgleichbetaalphagleich} that the corresponding pair $(\beta,\alpha)=(\beta(\omega_1),\alpha(\omega_1))\in [0,\infty)^2$ is uniquely determined by $\omega_1$. Hence, we may define a mapping $Y\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\to[0,\infty]^4$ as follows: if $\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\omega_4)\in\Omega_\Theta$, then we set $Y(\omega)=( \omega_1,\beta(\omega_1),\alpha(\omega_1),\omega_4)$; otherwise, if $\omega\in[0,\infty]^4\backslash\Omega_\Theta$, then we set $Y(\omega)=\omega$. As $\Theta$, and thus $\Omega_\Theta$, is a finite set, the mapping $Y$ is $\BBB([0,\infty]^4)/\BBB([0,\infty]^4)$-measurable. In view of \eqref{hsgleichbetaalphagleich}, note that $Q^Y_\theta=\widehat Q_\theta$ for all $\theta\in\Theta$ and thus $\delta(\FFF(\Theta),\widehat\FFF(\Theta))=0$, by~\eqref{defMarkov}. Second, assume that \eqref{hsgleichbetaalphagleich} is violated. There then exist some $h_0 > 0$, $\theta_1=(h_{0},\beta_1,\alpha_2,\lambda_1)$ $\in\Theta\cap\Theta_{e}\cap\widehat\Theta_{e}^C$ and $\theta_2=(h_{0},\beta_2,\alpha_2,\lambda_2)\in\Theta\cap\Theta_{e}$ such that $(\beta_1,\alpha_{1})\neq(\beta_2,\alpha_{2})$. Consider $\Theta_{0}=\{\theta_{1},\theta_{2}\}$ and the decision space $D=\{(\beta_1,\alpha_1),(\beta_2,\alpha_2)\}$, endowed with the discrete topology. For $\theta=(h_0,\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in\Theta$, consider (continuous and bounded) loss functions $W_\theta\dvtx D\to\RR$, where for $x=(x_1,\dots,x_4)\in[0,\infty]^4$, we set $W_{\theta}(x)=1-1_{\{(\beta,\alpha)\}}(x_2,x_3)$. Further, we define a Markov kernel $\widehat\rho\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\times\BBB(D)\to[0,1]$, where for $x\in[0,\infty]^4$ and $B\in\BBB(D)$, we set \[ \widehat\rho(x,B) = \cases{ \epsilon_{(\beta_1,\alpha_1)}(B) ,&\quad if $x\in(0,\infty)\times \{\beta_1\}\times\{\alpha_1\}\times[0,\infty)$,\cr \epsilon_{(\beta_2,\alpha_2)}(B) ,&\quad otherwise. } \] We then have $\int W_{\theta_i}(x) \widehat\rho(\omega,\mathrm{d}x) \widehat Q_{\theta_i}(\mathrm{d}\omega)=0$ for $i = 1,2$. On the other hand, any Markov kernel $\rho\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\times\BBB(D)\to[0,1]$ is of the form $\rho(\omega,B)=p(\omega)\epsilon_{(\beta_1,\alpha_1)}(B)+ (1-p(\omega))\epsilon_{(\beta_2,\alpha_2)}(B)$, where $p\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\to[0,1]$ is Borel, $\omega\in[0,\infty]^4$ and $B\in\BBB(D)$. It is easy to see that for such a Markov kernel $\rho$, there exists a Markov kernel $ \bar\rho\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\times \BBB(D)\to[0,1]$ such that both \[ \int W_{\theta_1}(x) \rho(\omega,\mathrm{d}x) Q_{\theta_1}(\mathrm{d}\omega)\ge \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma} \bigl(1-p(h_0,\infty,\infty,\infty)\bigr) \] and \[ \hspace*{-22pt}\int W_{\theta_2}(x) \rho(\omega,\mathrm{d}x) Q_{\theta_2}(\mathrm{d}\omega)\ge \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma}p(h_0,\infty,\infty,\infty) . \] In view of \eqref{defdeffic}, we thus have $\delta(\FFF(\Theta),\widehat\FFF(\Theta))\ge \delta(\FFF(\Theta_0),\FFF(\Theta_0))\ge \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma}/2$, which completes the proof of (ii). (iii) This follows by the same arguments as in (ii).
nodes.statement_short: Map $\widehat\FFF$ onto $\FFF$ and $\FFF_n$ by measurable relabelling; when the uniqueness condition fails, a two-point testing problem forces $\delta\ge \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma}/2$.

nodes.name: Part (i): $\widehat Q^X_\theta=Q_\theta$ gives zero deficiency
nodes.statement: By definition, the deficiency is non-decreasing in the parameter set with respect to set inclusions. Further, we have $\widehat Q^X_{\theta}=Q_{\theta}$ and $\widehat Q^{X_n}_{\theta}= Q_{\theta,n}$ for all $n\in\NN$ and thus, by~\eqref{defMarkov}, $\delta(\widehat\FFF(\Theta),\FFF(\Theta))\le \delta(\widehat\FFF,\FFF)=0$ and $\delta(\widehat\FFF(\Theta),\FFF_n(\Theta))\le \delta(\widehat\FFF,\FFF_n)=0$ for all $n\in\NN$, completing the proof of (i).
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity of deficiency in the parameter set then yields (i).

nodes.name: Part (ii), sufficiency: build $Y$ under the uniqueness condition
nodes.statement: (ii) First, assume that $\Theta$ satisfies \eqref{hsgleichbetaalphagleich} for all $x>0$. Without loss of generality, we may assume that $\Theta\subseteq[0,\infty)^4$ is a finite set (see \cite{St85}, Theorem 51.4). Define $\Omega_\Theta$ to be the set of all $\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\omega_4) \in(0,\infty)\times\{\infty\}^2\times\{0,\infty\}$ such that $( \omega_1,\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in(\Theta\cap\Theta_e)\backslash \widehat\Theta_e$ for some $(\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in[0,\infty)^3$. If $\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\omega_4)\in\Omega_\Theta$, then it follows from \eqref{hsgleichbetaalphagleich} that the corresponding pair $(\beta,\alpha)=(\beta(\omega_1),\alpha(\omega_1))\in [0,\infty)^2$ is uniquely determined by $\omega_1$. Hence, we may define a mapping $Y\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\to[0,\infty]^4$ as follows: if $\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\omega_4)\in\Omega_\Theta$, then we set $Y(\omega)=( \omega_1,\beta(\omega_1),\alpha(\omega_1),\omega_4)$; otherwise, if $\omega\in[0,\infty]^4\backslash\Omega_\Theta$, then we set $Y(\omega)=\omega$. As $\Theta$, and thus $\Omega_\Theta$, is a finite set, the mapping $Y$ is $\BBB([0,\infty]^4)/\BBB([0,\infty]^4)$-measurable. In view of \eqref{hsgleichbetaalphagleich}, note that $Q^Y_\theta=\widehat Q_\theta$ for all $\theta\in\Theta$ and thus $\delta(\FFF(\Theta),\widehat\FFF(\Theta))=0$, by~\eqref{defMarkov}.
nodes.statement_short: If $(\beta,\alpha)$ is determined by $h_0$ on $\Theta\cap\Theta_e$, a measurable relabelling maps $Q_\theta$ to $\widehat Q_\theta$.

nodes.name: Part (ii), necessity: two-point testing lower bound
nodes.statement: Second, assume that \eqref{hsgleichbetaalphagleich} is violated. There then exist some $h_0 > 0$, $\theta_1=(h_{0},\beta_1,\alpha_2,\lambda_1)$ $\in\Theta\cap\Theta_{e}\cap\widehat\Theta_{e}^C$ and $\theta_2=(h_{0},\beta_2,\alpha_2,\lambda_2)\in\Theta\cap\Theta_{e}$ such that $(\beta_1,\alpha_{1})\neq(\beta_2,\alpha_{2})$. Consider $\Theta_{0}=\{\theta_{1},\theta_{2}\}$ and the decision space $D=\{(\beta_1,\alpha_1),(\beta_2,\alpha_2)\}$, endowed with the discrete topology. For $\theta=(h_0,\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in\Theta$, consider (continuous and bounded) loss functions $W_\theta\dvtx D\to\RR$, where for $x=(x_1,\dots,x_4)\in[0,\infty]^4$, we set $W_{\theta}(x)=1-1_{\{(\beta,\alpha)\}}(x_2,x_3)$. Further, we define a Markov kernel $\widehat\rho\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\times\BBB(D)\to[0,1]$, where for $x\in[0,\infty]^4$ and $B\in\BBB(D)$, we set \[ \widehat\rho(x,B) = \cases{ \epsilon_{(\beta_1,\alpha_1)}(B) ,&\quad if $x\in(0,\infty)\times \{\beta_1\}\times\{\alpha_1\}\times[0,\infty)$,\cr \epsilon_{(\beta_2,\alpha_2)}(B) ,&\quad otherwise. } \] We then have $\int W_{\theta_i}(x) \widehat\rho(\omega,\mathrm{d}x) \widehat Q_{\theta_i}(\mathrm{d}\omega)=0$ for $i = 1,2$. On the other hand, any Markov kernel $\rho\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\times\BBB(D)\to[0,1]$ is of the form $\rho(\omega,B)=p(\omega)\epsilon_{(\beta_1,\alpha_1)}(B)+ (1-p(\omega))\epsilon_{(\beta_2,\alpha_2)}(B)$, where $p\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\to[0,1]$ is Borel, $\omega\in[0,\infty]^4$ and $B\in\BBB(D)$. It is easy to see that for such a Markov kernel $\rho$, there exists a Markov kernel $ \bar\rho\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\times \BBB(D)\to[0,1]$ such that both \[ \int W_{\theta_1}(x) \rho(\omega,\mathrm{d}x) Q_{\theta_1}(\mathrm{d}\omega)\ge \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma} \bigl(1-p(h_0,\infty,\infty,\infty)\bigr) \] and \[ \hspace*{-22pt}\int W_{\theta_2}(x) \rho(\omega,\mathrm{d}x) Q_{\theta_2}(\mathrm{d}\omega)\ge \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma}p(h_0,\infty,\infty,\infty) . \] In view of \eqref{defdeffic}, we thus have $\delta(\FFF(\Theta),\widehat\FFF(\Theta))\ge \delta(\FFF(\Theta_0),\FFF(\Theta_0))\ge \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma}/2$, which completes the proof of (ii).
nodes.statement_short: When uniqueness fails, a $0$–$1$ loss decision problem forces $\delta\ge\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma}/2$.

nodes.name: Part (iii) by the same arguments
nodes.statement: (iii) This follows by the same arguments as in (ii).
nodes.statement_short: The discrete-time version follows identically.

nodes.name: (Statistical) experiment
nodes.statement: Let $\Theta$ be a non-empty set, $(E,\AAA)$ be a measurable space and $(P_{\theta})_{\theta\in\Theta}$ be a family of probability measures on $\AAA$. The triplet $\EEE=(E,\AAA,(P_{\theta})_{\theta\in\Theta})$ is then called a~(statistical) experiment.
nodes.statement_short: A measurable space together with a $\Theta$-indexed family of probability measures on it.
differentia: $(P_{\theta})_{\theta\in\Theta}$ be a family of probability measures on $\AAA$

nodes.name: Decision problem
nodes.statement: A decision problem is a triple $(\Theta,D,W)$, where $D$ is a topological space and $W=(W_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ is a loss function $W_\theta\dvtx D\to\RR$, $\theta\in\Theta$. Let $\|W_\theta\|_{\infty}=\sup_{d\in D}|W_\theta(d)|$.

nodes.name: $\epsilon$-deficiency
nodes.statement: Also, let $\epsilon\ge0$. Then, $\EEE_1$ is called $\epsilon$-\textit{deficient with respect to} $\EEE_2$, notated as $\EEE_1\supseteq_\epsilon \EEE_2$, if and only if for all decision problems $(\Theta,D,W)$ with $W$ continuous and bounded, and all $\beta_2\in\BBB(\EEE_2,D)$, there exists some $\beta_1\in\BBB(\EEE_1,D)$ such that\looseness=-1 \[ \beta_1(W_\theta,P_{1,\theta})\le\beta_2(W_\theta,P_{2,\theta })+\epsilon\|W_\theta\|_{\infty} ,\qquad \theta\in\Theta , \]\looseness=0 where $\BBB(\EEE_i,D)$ ($i=1,2$) is the space of generalized decision functions (see \cite{St85}, Definition~42.2).
nodes.statement_short: $\EEE_1\supseteq_\epsilon\EEE_2$ if every decision procedure in $\EEE_2$ can be matched in $\EEE_1$ up to $\epsilon\|W_\theta\|_\infty$.

nodes.name: Deficiency $\delta(\EEE_1,\EEE_2)$
nodes.statement: The deficiency of $\EEE_1$ with respect to $\EEE_2$ is the number \begin{equation} \delta(\EEE_1,\EEE_2) = \inf\{\epsilon>0 \dvtx \EEE_1\supseteq _\epsilon \EEE_2\} . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The infimum of the $\epsilon$ for which $\EEE_1$ is $\epsilon$-deficient with respect to $\EEE_2$.
nodes.definiendum: The deficiency of $\EEE_1$ with respect to $\EEE_2$

nodes.name: Interpretation of $\EEE_1\supseteq_\epsilon\EEE_2$
nodes.statement: The relation $\EEE_1\supseteq_\epsilon \EEE_2$ is interpreted in the following sense: we have $\EEE_1\supseteq_\epsilon\EEE_2$ if $\EEE_1$ is more informative than $\EEE_2$ uniformly over all decision problems with continuous and bounded loss functions up to some error $\epsilon$.

nodes.name: Equivalence in deficiency
nodes.statement: Two experiments $\EEE_1$ and $\EEE_2$ are called \textit{equivalent in deficiency} if and only if $\EEE_1\supseteq_0 \EEE_2$ and $\EEE_2\supseteq_0 \EEE_1$.

nodes.name: Markov-kernel representation of the deficiency
nodes.statement: Recall that (see \cite{St85}, Lemma 55.4 and Remark 55.6(2)) \begin{equation} \delta(\EEE_1,\EEE_2) = \inf_K \sup_{\theta\in\Theta} \| P_{2,\theta} - K P_{1,\theta} \| \end{equation} with infimum now taken over all Markov kernels $K\dvtx E_1\times\EEE_2\to [0,1]$.
nodes.statement_short: The deficiency equals the infimum over Markov kernels of the uniform total-variation distance $\|P_{2,\theta}-KP_{1,\theta}\|$.
conclusions: \delta(\EEE_1,\EEE_2) = \inf_K \sup_{\theta\in\Theta} \| P_{2,\theta} - K P_{1,\theta} \|

nodes.name: Le Cam's distance $\Delta(\EEE_1,\EEE_2)$
nodes.statement: Le Cam's distance between $\EEE_1$ and $\EEE_2$ is a pseudo-metric on the space of all experiments indexed by $\Theta$ (see \cite{St85}, Corollary 59.6), defined by setting \begin{equation} \Delta(\EEE_1,\EEE_2) = \max\{ \delta(\EEE_1,\EEE_2),\delta(\EEE_2,\EEE_1) \}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The symmetrized deficiency $\max\{\delta(\EEE_1,\EEE_2),\delta(\EEE_2,\EEE_1)\}$, a pseudo-metric on experiments.
nodes.genus: a pseudo-metric on the space of all experiments indexed by $\Theta$

nodes.name: Total-variation bound for Le Cam's distance
nodes.statement: If $(E_1,\AAA_1)=(E_2,\AAA_2)$, then we have (see \cite{St85}, Corollary 59.6) \begin{equation} \Delta(\EEE_1,\EEE_2) \le \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|P_{1,\theta}-P_{2,\theta}\| . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: On a common sample space, $\Delta$ is dominated by the uniform total-variation distance between the two families.
conclusions: \Delta(\EEE_1,\EEE_2) \le \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|P_{1,\theta}-P_{2,\theta}\| .

nodes.name: Equivalence in deficiency iff $\Delta=0$
nodes.statement: Clearly, if $\EEE_1$ and $\EEE_2$ are two experiments indexed by the same $\Theta$, then $\EEE_1$ is equivalent to $\EEE_2$ in deficiency if and only if $\Delta(\EEE_1,\EEE_2)=0$.
assumptions: if $\EEE_1$ and $\EEE_2$ are two experiments indexed by the same $\Theta$
conclusions: $\EEE_1$ is equivalent to $\EEE_2$ in deficiency if and only if $\Delta(\EEE_1,\EEE_2)=0$

nodes.name: Convergence and asymptotic equivalence in deficiency
nodes.statement: Let $\EEE$, $\EEE_n$, $\FFF_n$, $n\in\NN$, be experiments, all indexed by $\Theta$. We then say that $\EEE_n$ converges (strongly) in deficiency, or that $\EEE_n$ and~$\FFF_n$ are (strongly) asymptotically equivalent in deficiency, if and only if $\Delta(\EEE_n,\EEE) \to0$ and $\Delta(\EEE_n,\FFF_n) \to0$, respectively, as $n\to\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Strong convergence / asymptotic equivalence in deficiency mean $\Delta(\EEE_n,\EEE)\to0$ / $\Delta(\EEE_n,\FFF_n)\to0$.

nodes.name: Subexperiments and weak convergence in deficiency
nodes.statement: For $\varnothing\neq\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, we employ the notation $\EEE(\Theta_0)=(E,\AAA,(P_{\theta})_{\theta_\in\Theta_0})$ for corresponding subexperiments of $\EEE=(E,\AAA,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$. We refer to weak convergence and weak asymptotic equivalence in deficiency if and only if, for all non-empty and finite $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, the corresponding subexperiments converge strongly and are strongly asymptotically equivalent in deficiency, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Restricting the parameter set gives subexperiments; weak notions require the strong ones for all finite parameter subsets.
